entities.summary:
Joseph Rabban, a pivotal figure in the history of the Malabar Coast, was a prominent Jewish merchant and aristocrat in early 11th-century Kodungallur (Muyirikode), then a flourishing entrepôt. His enduring significance stems from the Jewish Copper Plate Charter of Cochin, granted to him and his descendants by the Chera Perumal king Bhaskara Ravivarman I between 1000 and 1020 CE. This charter, inscribed on copper plates, bestowed upon Rabban and his lineage extensive hereditary rights, including sovereign privileges, feudal authority over land and its inhabitants, and exemption from certain taxes, effectively establishing a principality within the Chera kingdom.

The charter itself, a testament to the Chera rulers' policy of fostering trade and religious pluralism, delineated a remarkable array of powers for Rabban. These included the right to collect tolls, use a palanquin, ride an elephant, wear ceremonial lamps, and be heralded by drums—privileges typically reserved for high-ranking nobility or even minor kings. He was also granted the village of Anjuvannam and its surrounding lands, along with the right to levy taxes and administer justice. This unprecedented grant not only elevated Joseph Rabban to a position of immense local power but also provided a legal framework for the self-governance and protection of the Jewish community in Kodungallur, a crucial node in the Indian Ocean trade network.
